sourceAvailability.detail: Repository contains no Markdown, CSV, PDF, DOCX or plain-text requirements document. A full-tree search for non-source files returned only firebase.json, firestore.indexes.json and Asset catalogue Contents.json. No README, no docs/ directory prior to this audit. The sibling FridgeFit.zip in the parent directory is an archive of this same repository and contains no requirements document either.

Full recursive read of 89 production Swift files (7,760 lines) and 25 test files (3,472 lines), plus Config.xcconfig, Secrets.example.xcconfig, Info.plist, firestore.rules, firebase.json, .gitignore and FridgeFit.xcodeproj/project.pbxproj. 26 commits of git history reviewed.
sourceAvailability.impact: Implementation evidence is first-hand and complete.

sourceAvailability.detail: Xcode 26.1 (17B55) with iOS 26.1 simulator SDK and an iPhone 17 Pro (iOS 26.1) simulator present, matching the project's IPHONEOS_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET of 26.1. The unit test suite was executed on this simulator; the result is recorded in the testExecution block.
sourceAvailability.impact: Unit-level behaviour is verifiable. Device-only behaviour is not: the simulator provides no Apple Intelligence system language model, no physical camera, and this audit used no live Firebase or OpenRouter credentials.

testExecution.command: xcodebuild test -project FridgeFit.xcodeproj -scheme FridgeFit -destination 'platform=iOS Simulator,name=iPhone 17 Pro,OS=26.1' CODE_SIGNING_ALLOWED=NO

buildWarnings.theme: Swift concurrency: 'call to main actor-isolated X in a synchronous nonisolated context'. A consequence of the target building with SWIFT_DEFAULT_ACTOR_ISOLATION = MainActor while SWIFT_VERSION is still 5.0, so these are warnings today and would be errors under Swift 6 language mode.

testExecution.note: The full suite was executed, not merely counted: xcodebuild reported ** TEST SUCCEEDED ** with 240 'Test case ... passed' lines, zero failures and zero skips. The 240 figure matches the static count of `func test_` methods across 23 XCTest classes. The suite uses XCTest exclusively; no swift-testing (@Test) macros are present. The whole suite runs in under three seconds because every external dependency is behind a double.
testExecution.whatThisDoesNotProve: All 240 tests run against test doubles. The run involved no live Firebase project, no live OpenRouter request, no camera and no Apple Intelligence system language model (the Simulator provides none). A green suite here says the domain logic is correct; it says nothing about the four production integrations.

architecture.summary: SwiftUI + MVVM over an explicit Domain / Use Case / Repository separation. Views hold no business logic; view models hold no decisions; use cases own every rule; protocols isolate every external dependency so each one has a test double.

layers.name: Presentation (SwiftUI)
layers.detail: 16 view files across Pantry, Recipes, Scanner, Profile, Support. Root is FridgeFitApp -> LoginView | ContentView (3-tab TabView, one NavigationStack per tab).

layers.name: View Models (MVVM, @MainActor ObservableObject)
layers.detail: 5 view models: Auth, Pantry, Recipe, RecipeSuggestion, ReceiptScanner, Substitution. Each maps use-case results to renderable state and nothing more.

layers.name: Use Cases (Domain logic)
layers.detail: 12 use-case / policy types. All validation, feasibility, canonicalisation, normalisation, dedupe and ranking lives here.

layers.name: Domain (Models, Protocols, Errors)
layers.detail: 21 models, 6 protocols, 7 LocalizedError types. Protocols are the seam: PantryRepository, RecipeRepository, RecipeSuggestionService, ReceiptTextRecognizer, ReceiptIngredientInterpreter, SubstitutionService.

layers.name: Data (Adapters)
layers.detail: Firestore, Vision, FoundationModels and OpenRouter adapters, each behind a domain protocol, each paired with an in-memory or mock double used by previews and tests.

trustBoundary.principle: No generative model is permitted to assert pantry state. Every model output enters the app as an untrusted Raw* value and must pass a deterministic validator before any view sees it.

statusDefinitions.completed: Implemented, wired into the UI, exercised by automated tests that were executed in this audit, and no required integration is missing.
statusDefinitions.partial: Core implementation exists and is reachable, but an important requirement, integration or configuration is missing.
statusDefinitions.not_started: No meaningful implementation evidence found in the repository.
statusDefinitions.needs_verification: Implementation exists and looks correct on inspection, but correctness cannot be established here because it needs a physical device, live credentials, or runtime evidence this audit did not obtain.
statusDefinitions.blocked: Completion depends on a specific unresolved external dependency.

requirements.name: Email & password registration
requirements.description: A new user can create a FridgeFit account with an email address and password, and is signed in immediately afterwards.
requirements.evidence: RegisterView collects email, password and confirmation and calls AuthViewModel.signUp, which calls Auth.auth().createUser(withEmail:password:) and publishes the resulting user. The sheet dismisses itself only once isAuthenticated is true. Errors surface as error.localizedDescription in the form.
requirements.missing: No automated test of any kind covers AuthViewModel. No runtime evidence of a successful registration against the live Firebase project was produced in this audit.
requirements.remaining: Add AuthViewModel unit tests behind an injectable auth abstraction (Auth.auth() is called as a global singleton today, so the type is not testable as written). Then confirm one real registration end to end.
requirements.risks: AuthViewModel reaches Auth.auth() directly in init and in every method, which is why it has no tests. Making it testable is a small refactor of production code and therefore out of scope for this audit.
requirements.caveats: GoogleService-Info.plist is gitignored, so a fresh clone cannot authenticate at all until the Firebase config is supplied.

requirements.name: Email & password sign-in
requirements.description: A returning user signs in with email and password and lands on the authenticated app.
requirements.evidence: LoginView gates its submit button on non-empty email and password and on !isLoading, shows a ProgressView while in flight, and renders authViewModel.errorMessage inline. AuthViewModel.signIn calls Auth.auth().signIn(withEmail:password:).
requirements.missing: No tests; no executed runtime evidence.
requirements.remaining: Same injectable-auth refactor as CD-AUTH-01, then a sign-in unit test and one manual confirmation.
requirements.risks: Low implementation risk; the flow is conventional.
requirements.caveats: Email format is not validated client-side; a malformed address produces a Firebase error string rather than inline guidance.

requirements.name: Google Sign-In via Firebase Auth
requirements.description: The user can sign in with a Google account instead of email and password.
requirements.evidence: GoogleSignInButton on LoginView calls AuthViewModel.signInWithGoogle, which resolves the key window's root view controller, presents GIDSignIn, extracts the ID token, builds a GoogleAuthProvider credential and signs in to Firebase. FridgeFitApp configures GIDConfiguration from the Firebase clientID at launch and forwards callback URLs via onOpenURL. The reversed-client URL scheme is registered in Info.plist.
requirements.missing: No tests; no executed runtime evidence. The Google OAuth flow cannot be exercised without the gitignored GoogleService-Info.plist and a consenting Google account.
requirements.remaining: Confirm one real Google sign-in on a device or simulator with the Firebase config in place.
requirements.risks: The presenting-view-controller lookup uses first(where: isKeyWindow) on connectedScenes. This is the common pattern but can fail in multi-scene or iPad split-view contexts, in which case the user sees 'Unable to find a view to present Google Sign-In.'
requirements.caveats: Explicit failure messages exist for both the missing-presenter and missing-ID-token cases, so neither fails silently.

requirements.name: Session persistence and auth-state routing
requirements.description: A signed-in session survives app relaunch, and the root of the app switches between the login screen and the authenticated tabs automatically.
requirements.evidence: AuthViewModel seeds user from Auth.auth().currentUser in init and registers addStateDidChangeListener, removing the handle in deinit. FridgeFitApp's WindowGroup renders ContentView or LoginView on isAuthenticated, so the switch is driven by Firebase's own state rather than by navigation.
requirements.missing: No tests; relaunch persistence not demonstrated at runtime in this audit.
requirements.remaining: Confirm relaunch persistence manually, and confirm the pantry re-scopes correctly after an account switch.
requirements.risks: ContentView builds FirestorePantryRepository once in init. The repository reads Auth.auth().currentUser?.uid lazily on every call, so it does follow an account change; but ContentView's @StateObject view models are not rebuilt on sign-out/sign-in within one app session, so stale in-memory lists and the SubstitutionCache could outlive a user switch. This is a real, untested scenario.
requirements.caveats: Worth explicitly testing: sign out, sign in as a different user, and confirm the Pantry tab shows the second user's data.

requirements.name: Sign out
requirements.description: The user can sign out, which returns the app to the login screen and clears the Google session.
requirements.evidence: ProfileView's destructive Sign Out button calls AuthViewModel.signOut, which calls Auth.auth().signOut(), GIDSignIn.sharedInstance.signOut() and clears user, causing the root Group to render LoginView.
requirements.missing: No tests; no executed runtime evidence.
requirements.remaining: Confirm manually, including the account-switch case described in CD-AUTH-04.
requirements.risks: See CD-AUTH-04 regarding view-model and cache lifetime across a sign-out within one session.
requirements.caveats: No confirmation prompt before signing out, which is a deliberate-looking choice rather than a defect.

requirements.name: Registration input validation
requirements.description: The registration form validates input before submitting, rather than relying on backend errors.
requirements.evidence: RegisterView.validationError enforces a minimum password length of 6 and password/confirmation equality, and suppresses the message until the user has typed something. canSubmit additionally requires a non-empty email and no in-flight request.
requirements.missing: No email-format validation and no password-strength feedback beyond the 6-character floor. Validation lives in the View rather than in a use case, so it is the only rule in the app that cannot be unit tested without a UI test.
requirements.remaining: Add email-format validation; consider extracting the rules into a small testable type to match the pattern used everywhere else in this codebase.
requirements.risks: Low.
requirements.caveats: 6 characters matches Firebase's own default minimum, so the floor is not arbitrary.

requirements.name: Password reset / forgot password
requirements.description: A user who has forgotten their password can request a reset email and regain access to their account.
requirements.evidence: No implementation found. A case-insensitive search for sendPasswordReset across all Swift sources returns nothing, and neither LoginView nor RegisterView offers a reset affordance.
requirements.missing: Entire feature: UI entry point, AuthViewModel method, Firebase sendPasswordReset(withEmail:) call, and success/failure messaging.
requirements.remaining: Add a 'Forgot password?' control to LoginView, an AuthViewModel.sendPasswordReset(email:) method wrapping Auth.auth().sendPasswordReset, and a confirmation state that does not disclose whether the address is registered.
requirements.risks: Account recovery is a baseline expectation for any email/password product; without it a forgotten password is unrecoverable from inside the app.
requirements.caveats: Whether this is in scope depends on the Notion Feature List, which could not be read.

requirements.name: Email verification
requirements.description: A newly registered email address is verified before the account is treated as fully established.
requirements.evidence: No implementation found. Searches for sendEmailVerification and isEmailVerified return nothing; registration signs the user straight in.
requirements.missing: Verification send, verification state display, and any gating based on verification status.
requirements.remaining: Decide whether verification is required at all, then send on registration and surface the unverified state on Profile.
requirements.risks: Unverified addresses make the password-reset path (CD-AUTH-07) less trustworthy.
requirements.caveats: Legitimately optional for a coursework-scope product; listed because it is absent, not because it is necessarily required.

requirements.name: Automated test coverage for authentication
requirements.description: Authentication behaviour is covered by automated tests.
requirements.evidence: No test file references AuthViewModel, LoginView or RegisterView. The 23 test classes cover use cases, parsers, validators, view models for Pantry/Recipe/Scanner/Substitution, and Firestore field mapping, but authentication is the one feature area with zero coverage.
requirements.missing: All authentication tests.
requirements.remaining: Introduce an auth-service protocol so AuthViewModel can be driven by a double, then test sign-in success, sign-in failure messaging, sign-up, sign-out and the loading flag.
requirements.risks: Authentication is the gate on every other feature and is currently the least verified part of the app.
requirements.caveats: This is the direct consequence of AuthViewModel depending on the Auth.auth() singleton; it is a design consequence, not an oversight in the test suite.

requirements.name: View the pantry
requirements.description: The signed-in user sees everything currently in their pantry, with category, icon and formatted quantity, plus a distinct loading state, empty state and pull-to-refresh.
requirements.evidence: PantryView renders a ProgressView while loading-and-empty, a ContentUnavailableView with Scan Receipt and Add Ingredient actions when genuinely empty, and otherwise an inset-grouped List of rows carrying a tinted category IconBadge, name, category and monospaced-digit quantity. Rows are accessibility-combined with an explicit label and hint. .task loads on appear and .refreshable reloads on pull. PantryViewModel.loadItems toggles isLoading and maps failure into errorMessage.
requirements.missing: Nothing required for this requirement.
requirements.remaining: None.
requirements.risks: None identified.
requirements.caveats: The load-error alert is suppressed while any sheet is presented, so a failure that occurs behind a sheet is shown only after dismissal.

requirements.name: Add a pantry item with validation
requirements.description: The user adds an ingredient by name, category, quantity and unit. Blank names and negative quantities are rejected with a message written for the user.
requirements.evidence: AddPantryItemView is a pure form; AddPantryItemUseCase.execute trims the name, rejects empty with .emptyIngredientName, rejects quantity < 0 with .invalidQuantity, then constructs the PantryItem and persists it. A non-numeric quantity field becomes -1 in the view and is therefore rejected by the same rule rather than by a second one. Validation sits in the use case, so no caller can bypass it.
requirements.missing: Nothing required for this requirement.
requirements.remaining: None.
requirements.risks: None identified.
requirements.caveats: Quantity zero is deliberately allowed ('I have none left but still track it'), which is asserted by a dedicated test.

requirements.name: Duplicate prevention with guided recovery
requirements.description: Adding an ingredient the pantry already holds is rejected rather than silently merged, and the user is offered the update-the-existing-item path instead.
requirements.evidence: AddPantryItemUseCase matches against the existing pantry with Ingredient.matches(name:) (trimmed, case-insensitive) and throws .duplicateIngredient(name:). PantryViewModel catches that specific case and publishes duplicateItem; AddPantryItemView then renders an 'Update Existing Quantity' button which hands the item back to PantryView to present UpdatePantryItemView.
requirements.missing: Nothing required for this requirement.
requirements.remaining: None.
requirements.risks: None identified.
requirements.caveats: Matching is on the display name only. The canonical identity produced by IngredientCanonicalizer during a receipt scan is not used for pantry duplicate detection, so a hand-typed 'Bell Pepper' and a scanned 'Red Capsicum' are two pantry rows even though the scanner knows they are one ingredient. This is a real inconsistency worth a decision.

requirements.name: Update an item's quantity and unit
requirements.description: The user corrects how much of an ingredient they have, and in what unit.
requirements.evidence: Tapping a row sets editingItem and presents UpdatePantryItemView pre-filled from the item. UpdatePantryItemUseCase re-applies the quantity rule, resolves the item by id, mutates quantity and unit, and persists through the repository, throwing .itemNotFound if it vanished in between.
requirements.missing: Nothing required for this requirement.
requirements.remaining: None.
requirements.risks: None identified.
requirements.caveats: UpdatePantryItemView seeds its text field by splitting item.formattedQuantity on a space, so a fractional quantity arrives pre-rounded to one decimal place by MeasurementUnit.formatted. Saving an untouched form can therefore write back a slightly rounded value. Minor, but real.

requirements.name: Remove a pantry item
requirements.description: The user removes an ingredient they have used up, with a distinct error if it was already gone.
requirements.evidence: PantryView's List uses .onDelete; RemovePantryItemUseCase verifies presence first and throws .pantryItemNotFound rather than treating a missing item as a silent no-op. PantryViewModel routes that into removalErrorMessage, which is a separate published property from errorMessage specifically so a removal alert cannot collide with a form's inline error; the alert's OK handler reloads the list.
requirements.missing: Nothing required for this requirement.
requirements.remaining: None.
requirements.risks: removeItems(at:) spawns one unstructured Task per offset and each reloads the list on completion. Deleting several rows in one gesture therefore issues concurrent deletes and interleaved reloads. The repository operations are id-scoped so the end state is correct, but the intermediate list can flicker and the reloads are redundant.
requirements.caveats: Not a correctness defect; worth tidying if multi-row deletion is a common path.

requirements.name: Per-user Firestore persistence
requirements.description: Each user's pantry persists in Cloud Firestore, scoped to their own Firebase UID, and is never readable or writable by another account.
requirements.evidence: FirestorePantryRepository resolves users/{uid}/pantry from an injectable userIDProvider that defaults to Auth.auth().currentUser?.uid, and throws PantryRepositoryError.notAuthenticated rather than ever falling back to an unscoped path. Reads are ordered by ingredientName. Creates write both createdAt and updatedAt as FieldValue.serverTimestamp(); updates deliberately omit createdAt so an edit cannot reset the creation time. Updates and deletes check document existence first and map to the domain's own itemNotFound / pantryItemNotFound errors. ContentView injects this repository into every pantry-touching view model, so this is the production path.
requirements.missing: Only the pure encode/decode helpers are tested. No test exercises fetchAll, add, update or remove against Firestore — not against a live project, and not against the Firebase Emulator Suite. The eight tests prove the field mapping is correct and self-consistent; they prove nothing about whether a write reaches Firestore.
requirements.remaining: Add Firebase Emulator Suite integration tests covering the four CRUD operations plus the notAuthenticated path, or record a documented manual end-to-end pass. firebase.json already exists, so emulator configuration is a short step.
requirements.risks: This is the project's single most important unverified integration: every other feature's persistence runs through it. A decode that silently returns nil (the compactMap in fetchAll drops undecodable documents without surfacing anything) would present as an item quietly disappearing from the pantry.
requirements.caveats: The injectable userIDProvider makes emulator testing straightforward — the seam already exists and is simply unused by the suite.

requirements.name: Firestore security rules scoping the pantry to its owner
requirements.description: Server-side rules guarantee a signed-in user can read and write only their own pantry, and everything else is denied.
requirements.evidence: firestore.rules matches /users/{uid}/pantry/{pantryItemId} and allows read, write only when request.auth != null && request.auth.uid == uid, followed by a catch-all /{document=**} deny. firebase.json points the firestore.rules and firestore.indexes.json keys at those files.
requirements.missing: No evidence the rules have ever been deployed to the Firebase project, and no rules unit tests. The repository contains the correct rules; it does not demonstrate that the live project enforces them.
requirements.remaining: Run `firebase deploy --only firestore:rules` against the project and add @firebase/rules-unit-testing cases asserting that user A cannot read user B's pantry.
requirements.risks: If the live project is still on default or test-mode rules, every user's pantry is readable by any authenticated client regardless of what this file says. The client-side uid scoping in FirestorePantryRepository is a correctness measure, not a security boundary.
requirements.caveats: The rules themselves read correctly and deny by default, which is the right shape.

requirements.name: Expiry date and freshness tracking
requirements.description: Pantry items carry an expiry or best-before date so the user can see what needs using up.
requirements.evidence: No implementation found. PantryItem holds only id, ingredient, quantity and unit. A case-insensitive search for expir / bestBefore / useBy / shelfLife across all production Swift sources returns only an unrelated comment in SubstitutionCache.
requirements.missing: Date field on PantryItem, Firestore field and migration for existing documents, form input, list sorting or badging, and any notification.
requirements.remaining: Add an optional expiryDate to PantryItem, extend the Firestore encode/decode pair and its mapping tests, surface it in the add/update forms and badge expiring rows in PantryView.
requirements.risks: Adding a field to the Firestore schema requires the decoder to tolerate documents written before the change. The current decoder uses strict guard-let on every field, so any new required field would silently drop all existing pantry items. The field must be optional.
requirements.caveats: Commonly expected of a pantry app, but its presence in the Notion Feature List could not be confirmed.

requirements.name: Pantry search, filter and sort controls
requirements.description: The user can search the pantry by name and filter or sort it, for example by category.
requirements.evidence: No implementation found. PantryView contains no .searchable modifier and no filter or sort state; a search across all Swift sources for searchable / searchText returns nothing. The only ordering is the Firestore query's fixed order(by: "ingredientName").
requirements.missing: Search field, filter controls, sort options and the corresponding view-model state.
requirements.remaining: Add .searchable plus a category filter to PantryView, with the filtering logic in the view model so it can be tested.
requirements.risks: Usability degrades as the pantry grows; a receipt scan can add ten items at once, so lists get long quickly.
requirements.caveats: Not confirmed as a requirement.

requirements.name: Offline behaviour and cache configuration
requirements.description: The pantry remains usable without a network connection, with a defined offline policy.
requirements.evidence: No implementation found. Firestore is used via the default Firestore.firestore() instance with no FirestoreSettings, no explicit cache configuration and no network-state handling. PantryViewModel surfaces any failure as error.localizedDescription with no offline-specific messaging or retry.
requirements.missing: An explicit offline decision. The Firestore SDK provides some local caching by default, but nothing here configures, relies on, tests or documents it, so no offline guarantee can be claimed.
requirements.remaining: Decide the offline policy, configure FirestoreSettings deliberately, and give the UI an offline-aware message distinct from a generic failure.
requirements.risks: A kitchen is exactly where connectivity is unreliable. Today a network failure produces a raw Firestore error string in an alert.
requirements.caveats: Listed as not started because no deliberate offline work exists, not because the SDK provides nothing.

requirements.name: Browse recipes
requirements.description: The user browses a list of recipes, each showing a feasibility badge and pantry coverage at a glance.
requirements.evidence: RecipeListView renders a List of RecipeRow, each with a feasibility-tinted IconBadge, the status title, matched/total counts and a coverage percentage, falling back to 'Checking pantry…' before evaluation completes. It has a loading state, a ContentUnavailableView empty state, pull-to-refresh bound to refreshFeasibility, and an error alert. RecipeViewModel.loadRecipes fetches through the RecipeRepository protocol and then evaluates every recipe.
requirements.missing: Nothing required for browsing itself.
requirements.remaining: None for this requirement; the data source is tracked separately as CD-RECIPE-05.
requirements.risks: RecipeListView calls loadRecipes from .onAppear, which fires on every tab return and re-fetches and re-evaluates the whole list each time. Harmless with 10 bundled recipes; it would need rethinking against a remote catalogue.
requirements.caveats: The catalogue is 10 hard-coded recipes compiled into the binary (BundledRecipeRepository.sampleRecipes). The code documents this as a phase decision and the RecipeRepository protocol is the seam for a remote source, but a reviewer should not read 'recipe browsing works' as 'a recipe backend exists'.

requirements.name: Recipe detail with ingredients and instructions
requirements.description: A recipe's full detail shows its summary, servings, each ingredient compared against the pantry, and numbered cooking steps.
requirements.evidence: RecipeDetailView renders summary and servings, a Feasibility section with status and coverage, an Ingredients section of RecipeIngredientRow built from the evaluated result, and numbered Instructions. RecipeIngredientRow renders availability-specific detail text — on-hand versus required, 'Need N more', 'Optional, missing', or 'Check amount' — and renders unresolved optional ingredients in a muted style so they cannot be mistaken for blockers. .task calls evaluateIfNeeded as a defensive fallback if the detail opens before the list's evaluation lands.
requirements.missing: Nothing required for this requirement.
requirements.remaining: None.
requirements.risks: None identified.
requirements.caveats: No images (see CD-RECIPE-07), no serving-size scaling, and no step-by-step cooking mode.

requirements.name: Recipe feasibility evaluation against the pantry
requirements.description: FridgeFit answers 'can I make this?' deterministically from the current pantry, distinguishing makeable, almost makeable and not makeable, and reporting coverage of essential ingredients.
requirements.evidence: EvaluateRecipeFeasibilityUseCase reads the pantry fresh on every call and classifies each ingredient as available, insufficient, missing, or quantityUnverified when the units cannot be safely converted — failing closed rather than guessing. Matching is by normalised name via Ingredient.matches(name:), the same rule Pantry uses, because recipe and pantry ids are generated independently and could never match. Status is a single documented rule: all essential available -> makeable; at least half available -> almostMakeable; otherwise notMakeable; a recipe with no essential ingredients is trivially makeable. Optional ingredients never affect the verdict. RecipeFeasibilityResult exposes the derived groupings and coveragePercentage so list row, detail screen and tests read one verdict.
requirements.missing: Nothing required for this requirement.
requirements.remaining: None.
requirements.risks: None identified. This is the most thoroughly tested rule in the codebase: 16 dedicated cases covering each status boundary, both conversion directions, the fail-closed path and the trivial case.
requirements.caveats: Name matching is exact-after-normalisation. 'Chicken' in the pantry does not satisfy a recipe's 'Chicken Breast', even though IngredientCanonicalizer would resolve both to 'chicken'. The canonicaliser is used only in the scan pipeline. See CD-PANTRY-03.

requirements.name: Unit conversion for quantity comparison
requirements.description: Pantry quantities are converted into the recipe's unit so amounts can be compared, without ever guessing an unsafe conversion.
requirements.evidence: MeasurementUnit.convert handles identity plus the four exact same-dimension conversions (g<->kg, ml<->L) and returns nil for everything else, which callers translate into quantityUnverified / unsupportedUnit rather than a guess. Seven tests cover identity, all four conversions, cross-dimension and unsupported pairs.
requirements.missing: MeasurementUnit offers eight units but only four participate in conversion. cups, tbsp, tsp and pcs can never be compared to anything but themselves, so a pantry entry of '2 cups' against a recipe needing '250 ml' is permanently 'Check amount'. Those four units are selectable in both the add and update forms and in the receipt review screen, so a user can readily create pantry items that feasibility can never evaluate.
requirements.remaining: Either add volume ratios for cup/tbsp/tsp (a cup is a defined volume; the ambiguity is ingredient density, not the unit), or restrict the unit pickers to the units the app can actually reason about, or label the unconvertible units in the picker.
requirements.risks: This is a gap between what the UI invites the user to enter and what the domain can evaluate. It degrades gracefully and honestly, which is the right failure mode, but the degradation is silent until the user reaches a recipe.
requirements.caveats: Failing closed is the correct design choice and is explicitly documented and tested. The gap is the unit set offered, not the conversion logic.

requirements.name: Remote recipe catalogue
requirements.description: Recipes come from a remote backend or API rather than a fixed dataset compiled into the app, so the catalogue can grow without shipping a new build.
requirements.evidence: No implementation found. The only RecipeRepository conformances are BundledRecipeRepository (10 hard-coded recipes) and InMemoryRecipeRepository (a test double). BundledRecipeRepository's own documentation states 'Phase 2 doesn't have a remote recipe API yet'. No networking code exists outside OpenRouterSubstitutionService.
requirements.missing: The entire remote source: API choice, a RecipeRepository conformance, response models, error mapping, caching and pagination.
requirements.remaining: Choose a source (a recipe API, or Firestore as the recipe store), implement RecipeRepository against it, and inject it in ContentView. The protocol boundary means no use case or view changes.
requirements.risks: A 10-recipe catalogue bounds how useful feasibility matching can be: most real pantries will not match any of the ten. This is the single biggest limitation on the product's core value proposition, independent of code quality.
requirements.caveats: The architecture is genuinely ready for this — a one-line change in ContentView — so the cost is in the adapter, not in the app.

requirements.name: Recipe search and filtering
requirements.description: The user can search recipes by name or ingredient and filter them, for example to show only makeable recipes.
requirements.evidence: No implementation found. RecipeListView has no .searchable and no filter state; recipes render in the repository's fixed order with no way to narrow them.
requirements.missing: Search field, filter controls and view-model support.
requirements.remaining: Add .searchable and a feasibility filter, with the predicate in RecipeViewModel so it is testable.
requirements.risks: Low while the catalogue is 10 recipes; becomes necessary alongside CD-RECIPE-05.
requirements.caveats: 'Show me only what I can make' is arguably the most valuable filter this app could offer, since the feasibility verdict is already computed for every recipe.

requirements.name: Recipe imagery
requirements.description: Recipes display a photograph or image rather than a generic icon.
requirements.evidence: No implementation found. Recipe carries an optional symbolName used as an SF Symbol, documented in the model as 'no photo pipeline in this phase'. The asset catalogue contains only AppIcon and AccentColor.
requirements.missing: Image URLs or assets, async loading, placeholder and failure states, and caching.
requirements.remaining: Add an image reference to Recipe and render with AsyncImage; most naturally delivered together with CD-RECIPE-05.
requirements.risks: Purely presentational.
requirements.caveats: SF Symbols are used consistently and legibly today, so the absence reads as a deliberate scope choice rather than an unfinished screen.

requirements.name: Favourites, saved recipes and cooking history
requirements.description: The user can save or favourite recipes and see what they have cooked before.
requirements.evidence: No implementation found. A search for favorite / favourite / markAsCooked across all production sources returns nothing. Firestore holds only the pantry subcollection.
requirements.missing: Domain model, Firestore collection and rules, use cases, and UI.
requirements.remaining: Add a users/{uid}/favourites subcollection with matching security rules, a repository and use case, and a toggle on RecipeDetailView.
requirements.risks: None; purely additive.
requirements.caveats: Not confirmed as a requirement.

requirements.name: Deduct ingredients from the pantry after cooking
requirements.description: Marking a recipe as cooked subtracts the ingredients it used from the pantry, closing the loop between recipes and pantry state.
requirements.evidence: No implementation found. No 'cook' or 'consume' action exists on RecipeDetailView, and no use case decrements pantry quantities. Quantities change only through UpdatePantryItemUseCase, driven by a manual form.
requirements.missing: A ConsumeRecipeIngredientsUseCase, unit-aware subtraction, a decision about what to do with unconvertible units and with quantities that would go negative, and a UI action.
requirements.remaining: Add the use case and a 'Cooked this' action; reuse MeasurementUnit.convert and refuse to deduct where conversion returns nil, consistent with how the rest of the app fails closed.
requirements.risks: This is what makes the pantry stay accurate over time. Without it, pantry quantities drift from reality the moment the user cooks anything, which in turn degrades every feasibility verdict and every AI suggestion. It is the highest-value missing feature found in this audit.
requirements.caveats: Not confirmed as a requirement, but it is the natural completion of the pantry/recipe loop the rest of the app is built around.

requirements.name: On-device recipe ideas generated from the pantry
requirements.description: The user gets recipe ideas generated from what is actually in their pantry, computed on-device with Apple Intelligence.
requirements.evidence: AppleRecipeSuggestionService uses FoundationModels guided generation into @Generable GeneratedRecipeIdeas (max 5 recipes, 2–12 ingredients each, temperature 0.4), with session instructions that forbid hiding a missing ingredient and forbid the model asserting pantry contents. SuggestRecipesFromPantryUseCase reads the pantry, calls the service and validates the result. RecipeSuggestionViewModel guards against concurrent runs with a monotonic token so a superseded request cannot publish, and distinguishes an empty result from an error. PantryRecipeIdeasView is presented as a sheet from the Recipes toolbar and renders unavailable, loading, error, empty and populated states. Wired in ContentView.
requirements.missing: Every test runs against MockRecipeSuggestionService. AppleRecipeSuggestionService itself — the @Generable schema, the SystemLanguageModel call, the availability mapping and the GenerationError mapping — has no test and was not executed in this audit. The iOS Simulator provides no system language model, so this code path cannot run there at all.
requirements.remaining: Run the feature on an Apple Intelligence-capable device with Apple Intelligence enabled, and record what the model actually returns for a representative pantry. Judge usefulness, latency and refusal behaviour from that evidence, not from the prompt.
requirements.risks: Device and OS gated: requires hardware eligible for Apple Intelligence (iPhone 15 Pro or later, or an M-series iPad/Mac), iOS 26.x, the feature enabled in Settings, and the model assets downloaded. On any other device the feature is permanently unavailable. The app handles this correctly (see CD-AI-03) but the capability is not universally available to users.
requirements.caveats: Prompt quality cannot be assessed statically. The instructions are well targeted at the known failure mode, but whether the model follows them is an empirical question this audit did not answer.

requirements.name: Pantry-authoritative availability split on suggestions
requirements.description: A suggestion's available-versus-missing ingredient split is computed from the real pantry, never taken from the model, so the app can never tell the user they have something they do not.
requirements.evidence: The @Generable schema deliberately has no 'available' or 'missing' field — the model is asked only what a recipe requires. SuggestRecipesFromPantryUseCase.validate recomputes both lists by matching required names against the real pantry with Ingredient.matches(name:), drops suggestions with a blank name or no ingredients, deduplicates required ingredients case-insensitively, drops suggestions that use nothing from the pantry, and normalises a zero-minute estimate to nil. RawRecipeSuggestion and RecipeSuggestion are separate types precisely so the untrusted and validated shapes cannot be confused.
requirements.missing: Nothing required for this requirement.
requirements.remaining: None.
requirements.risks: None identified. test_suggestRecipes_marksIngredientMissing_whenPantryDisagrees asserts the adversarial case directly: the model claims availability, the pantry disagrees, and the pantry wins.
requirements.caveats: The UI states this to the user in PantryRecipeIdeasView's footer, so the guarantee is visible rather than merely internal.

requirements.name: Apple Intelligence unavailable-state handling
requirements.description: When Apple Intelligence cannot run, the affected feature explains why in plain language and the rest of the app keeps working.
requirements.evidence: AppleIntelligenceAvailability models five states — available, appleIntelligenceNotEnabled, deviceNotSupported, modelNotReady, unavailableForUnknownReason — each with a user-facing title and explanation that never mentions a framework, and an unrecognised SDK reason maps to unavailableForUnknownReason and fails closed rather than assuming the feature works. Availability is re-read on every access so returning from Settings reflects the new state. PantryRecipeIdeasView and ReceiptScannerView both substitute a ContentUnavailableView and offer the manual path instead. Nothing in Pantry, Recipes or Firebase depends on this type.
requirements.missing: Nothing required for this requirement.
requirements.remaining: None.
requirements.risks: None identified. test_execute_doesNotRunOCR_whenScanningIsUnavailable asserts the availability check happens before any work, so an unavailable model does not cause the device to OCR a photo for nothing.
requirements.caveats: The mapping from SystemLanguageModel.Availability onto these cases is itself untested (it needs the real SDK type), so the five states are proven to behave correctly once set, but not proven to be set correctly on real hardware.

requirements.name: Acting on a generated suggestion
requirements.description: The user can do something with a suggestion they like — save it as a recipe, or add its missing ingredients to a shopping list.
requirements.evidence: No implementation found. SuggestionRow in PantryRecipeIdeasView is display-only: name, time, availability labels and instructions, with no action. No shopping-list type exists anywhere in the codebase.
requirements.missing: Any action on a suggestion, and the shopping-list or saved-recipe feature it would feed.
requirements.remaining: Decide the destination first (saved recipes per CD-RECIPE-08, or a shopping list), then add the action.
requirements.risks: Suggestions are currently transient — not persisted, and regenerated on every sheet open — so a useful idea is lost as soon as the sheet closes.
requirements.caveats: Not confirmed as a requirement.

requirements.name: Capture or choose a receipt photo
requirements.description: The user photographs a grocery receipt with the camera or picks an existing photo from their library.
requirements.evidence: ReceiptScannerView offers Take Photo and Choose from Library. The camera path resolves permission through CameraAccess.request() before presenting, distinguishing granted, denied and unavailable (no camera, e.g. Simulator) and showing an explanation rather than a black viewfinder. CameraPicker wraps UIImagePickerController and calls onFailure when a capture yields no usable image. The library path uses PhotosPicker, loading bytes off the main actor and reporting a load failure through the scanner's normal error surface. Both funnel into ReceiptScannerViewModel.selectImage, which cancels any in-flight scan so results cannot describe the previous photo.
requirements.missing: No automated coverage of CameraPicker, CameraAccess or the PhotosPicker path — all three are UIKit/PhotoKit integration points with no test double. Camera capture cannot be exercised on the Simulator.
requirements.remaining: Confirm on a physical device: capture, permission-denied, retake, and library selection including a HEIC photo and a non-image item.
requirements.risks: Scanning requires selectedImage.cgImage to be non-nil. Some library images (notably certain HEIC or CIImage-backed representations) have no backing CGImage, which would surface as 'That photo couldn't be read' for a photo the user can plainly see. Untested.
requirements.caveats: Permission is resolved before presentation, which is the correct order and avoids the common black-viewfinder bug.

requirements.name: On-device OCR of the receipt with row stitching
requirements.description: Vision reads the receipt's text on-device, in reading order, reassembling the description and price columns into single lines.
requirements.evidence: VisionReceiptTextRecognizer configures RecognizeTextRequest at .accurate with usesLanguageCorrection = false (deliberate, and the reasoning is documented: correction rewrites CHKN and CAPS toward real dictionary words and the interpreter then faithfully reads the wrong product), minimumTextHeightFraction lowered to 0.008 so small lines on a whole-receipt photo are not silently skipped, and recognitionLanguages asked of the request rather than hardcoded because forcing an unsupported identifier makes Vision throw. Full-resolution CGImage, no downsampling. Observations are sorted by descending midY (Vision's origin is bottom-left) and grouped into rows by vertical-centre proximity relative to row height, then ordered left-to-right and joined; a row's confidence is its least confident fragment, and rows below 0.3 are dropped. Image orientation is bridged from UIImage.Orientation so camera captures are not read sideways.
requirements.missing: VisionReceiptTextRecognizer has no tests at all. Every scan test uses MockReceiptTextRecognizer with pre-written lines, so the row-stitching geometry, the confidence floor, the language selection and the orientation bridge are entirely unexercised.
requirements.remaining: Add tests for the row-grouping function against synthetic observations (the geometry is pure and testable once the Vision types are constructed), and run the real recogniser against a set of photographed receipts to measure line recovery.
requirements.risks: Row stitching compares each fragment only against the most recent row, so fragments arriving out of expected order could start a spurious new row. The rowGroupingTolerance of 0.6 and confidence floor of 0.3 are unvalidated magic numbers — plausible, but no evidence supports them. OCR quality is the first link in the chain: a line lost here is invisible to the user, which is the exact failure mode the rest of the pipeline is designed to avoid.
requirements.caveats: The design decisions here are unusually well reasoned and documented. The gap is empirical validation, not design.

requirements.name: Deterministic receipt line parsing
requirements.description: OCR output is reduced to candidate product lines by removing receipt furniture — totals, payment lines, store metadata — and splitting the trailing price off each description, without modifying the original text.
requirements.evidence: ReceiptLineParser is a deliberately weak filter: it removes only what is unambiguously not a product, documenting that a wrongly dropped line is invisible to the user whereas a wrongly kept one costs one extra row the model will triage anyway. Metadata is matched as whole words so CASHEWS survives CASH and CARDAMOM survives CARD; multi-word phrases are matched as consecutive words; ambiguous leading words such as TOTAL are treated as metadata only when nothing alphabetic follows, so 'TOTAL 45.67' is dropped and 'TOTAL GREEK YOGURT 6.00' is kept. Price splitting works on the last whitespace-separated token and requires exactly two decimal places, which keeps 500G and 2L from being read as prices; a trailing tax flag token is tolerated. A leading 5+ digit barcode is stripped. A bare '2 @ $3.00' multiplier line is folded into the previous line rather than discarded. originalText is never modified.
requirements.missing: Nothing required for this requirement.
requirements.remaining: None.
requirements.risks: None identified. The substring-collision cases (CASHEWS/CASH, CARDAMOM/CARD) and the TOTAL-as-brand case are each asserted by a dedicated test.
requirements.caveats: The metadata word list is Australian-retailer oriented. A receipt from another market could leak more furniture through — which, by this parser's stated design, is the safe direction to fail.

requirements.name: Deterministic quantity extraction from receipt text
requirements.description: A quantity is read from the receipt line by scanning characters, never inferred, and 'the receipt did not say' is a real answer rather than a default.
requirements.evidence: ReceiptQuantityParser reads weight and volume suffixes (g/gm/gms/gr/grm, kg/kgs, ml/mls, L/lt/ltr), handling both '500G' and '500 G', and prefers weight or volume over a count because '2 @ CHKN 500G' means 500 g of chicken. A count is read only from an explicit '2 @' or '3 x' multiplier shape, deliberately ignoring a bare leading number because on receipts that is as often a line number or PLU as a quantity. Trailing punctuation left by OCR is tolerated. Returning nil is documented as the honest answer, which the UI renders as 'quantity not detected'. ReceiptQuantityParser.text(_:states:) exists specifically so a model-proposed number can be checked against the receipt text.
requirements.missing: Nothing required for this requirement.
requirements.remaining: None.
requirements.risks: None identified.
requirements.caveats: Pack counts written without a multiplier (for example 'EGGS 12PK') are not recognised as a quantity of 12, and correctly fall through to 'not detected' for the user to supply.

requirements.name: Apple Intelligence interpretation of receipt lines
requirements.description: The on-device language model reads each cleaned receipt line and says what was purchased, what kind of purchase it is, and its canonical ingredient name — seeing only text, never the photo.
requirements.evidence: AppleReceiptIngredientInterpreter sends ReceiptLineItems (text only; the photo never reaches the model) to SystemLanguageModel via guided generation into @Generable GeneratedReceiptInterpretation. The schema is designed around three decisions: no Optional properties (a not-stated quantity is 0 plus a notStated unit sentinel), enums rather than free strings for classification, category and unit so the model can only emit values the app understands, and originalText echoed back so each interpretation can be matched to the line it came from. Lines go in batches of 12 with a fresh session each, capped at 84 lines per receipt, at temperature 0.1 because creativity here means invented groceries. GenerationError is collapsed to actionable ReceiptScanErrors with details sent to the log rather than the screen. The prompt builder's instructions require one entry per line in order, forbid adding products, cover Australian abbreviations (CHKN, CAPS, MUSH, AVO, BNLS, W/MEAL, ATL), define all six classifications, make 'unknown' a first-class answer over a plausible guess, and forbid estimating or converting quantities.
requirements.missing: The 11 tests cover the prompt and instruction text; none covers the interpreter. The @Generable schema, the SystemLanguageModel call, the availability mapping, the GenerationError mapping and the batching loop were not executed, and cannot be on the Simulator.
requirements.remaining: Run real scans on an Apple Intelligence-capable device across several receipts and store formats. Measure how often the model echoes originalText exactly (the normaliser discards items it cannot match, so a paraphrasing model silently loses products), how often it returns one entry per line, and how it classifies ambiguous items such as milk and stock.
requirements.risks: Same device and OS gating as CD-AI-01. The architecture's main defence — echo matching — depends on the model copying each line back character for character, which is precisely the instruction a model is most likely to drift on. The normaliser's tolerant containment fallback mitigates this, but the real rate is unmeasured.
requirements.caveats: Asserting prompt content in tests is an unusual and genuinely useful choice: it guards the instructions that carry the safety properties against accidental edits.

requirements.name: Deterministic normalisation and anti-hallucination of model output
requirements.description: Every interpreted item is validated against the lines that were actually sent, so a product the model invented can never reach the pantry; survivors are canonicalised, quantity-resolved, deduplicated and split into pantry candidates and exclusions.
requirements.evidence: ReceiptItemNormalizer applies seven documented rules in order. The first is the hard stop: an item is matched back to a real receipt line through the model's echo, compared on folded text (uppercased alphanumerics only, tolerating spacing and punctuation drift), and discarded if no line corresponds — a model that decides a shopper probably bought milk has nowhere to attach the claim. Matched lines are consumed, so an echo repeated twice yields one candidate. Blank and over-60-character names are dropped; unrecognised classifications and categories fall back to .unknown and .other rather than being guessed. Quantity resolution runs the deterministic parser first and accepts the model's proposal only when the parser found nothing AND the proposed number literally appears in the line. Duplicates are collapsed by canonical name in receipt order, adding same-unit quantities (two 500 g chicken lines really is a kilogram) and keeping the first quantity when units differ rather than inventing a conversion. An item is excluded only if every line for it was non-ingredient. ReceiptItemClassification.shouldAddToPantry is the single place the product decision lives, and only .ingredient qualifies.
requirements.missing: Nothing required for this requirement.
requirements.remaining: None.
requirements.risks: None identified at unit level. The 25 tests are the most comprehensive set in the project and include the adversarial case directly (test_normalize_dropsItemsThatEchoALineNeverSent). The residual risk is upstream and is recorded under CD-SCAN-05: how often a real model echoes faithfully enough to be matched.
requirements.caveats: The containment fallback accepts a match only when exactly one remaining line contains the echo or is contained by it, which keeps the tolerance from becoming ambiguous.

requirements.name: Ingredient name canonicalisation
requirements.description: The same food arriving spelled several ways resolves to one stable internal identity, while the user keeps reading the receipt's own wording.
requirements.evidence: IngredientCanonicalizer runs a four-step pipeline: fold (lowercase, strip diacritics, turn _ - / into spaces, drop punctuation, delete apostrophes so za'atar stays one word); phrase lookup of the whole folded phrase and its singularised form against the synonym table BEFORE any words are removed, which is what protects compounds — 'sweet potato' is matched whole so descriptor removal never strips 'sweet' and merges it into 'potato'; descriptor removal of a conservative list of words that modify a food without changing which food it is, kept if removing them would leave nothing because 'cherry' alone is a fruit; then lookup again, falling back to the stripped phrase in snake_case so an unknown grocery still gets a stable identity. Display names keep the receipt's flavour ('Red Capsicum', not 'bell_pepper'), with a preferred-Australian-term fallback when the model returned something internal-looking. The model's canonical suggestion is treated as a hint that wins only when it resolves to a known name.
requirements.missing: Nothing required for this requirement as scoped to the scan pipeline.
requirements.remaining: None for the scan pipeline. Extending canonical identity to pantry duplicate detection and recipe matching is tracked under CD-PANTRY-03 and CD-RECIPE-03.
requirements.risks: The descriptor list merges names that were previously distinct, and a wrong merge is much harder for a user to notice than a missed one. The code says this explicitly and keeps the list conservative — notably omitting colour words like 'orange' that are also foods — and test_canonicalize_keepsUnrelatedFoodsApart guards the direction that matters.
requirements.caveats: The canonical identity is computed and stored on ReceiptIngredientCandidate but is NOT carried into PantryItem, so the work is used for scan-time deduplication only and is discarded at the pantry boundary. That is the root of the inconsistency noted in CD-PANTRY-03.

requirements.name: Review and correct detected items before saving
requirements.description: Nothing is stored until the user confirms it. Every detected row can be renamed, recategorised, requantified, unticked or deleted first, with the originating receipt line shown so the user can check it against the paper.
requirements.evidence: ReceiptItemReviewView lists one editable ReceiptItemRow per draft with a tick, an editable name field, the source receipt line, and quantity, unit and category pickers; swipe-to-delete removes a row. ReceiptScannerViewModel owns the drafts and exposes toggleSelection, updateName, updateCategory, updateQuantityText, updateUnit, removeDraft and removeDrafts. A row with no detected quantity starts with an empty field and says 'Quantity not detected — enter one to add this item' rather than being pre-filled with a made-up '1 pcs'; an item already in the pantry starts unticked and warns why. Two things are deliberately absent and documented: no confidence badge (the old fridge-scan showed the model's self-reported confidence, which measured nothing and gave the user no action) and no canonical identifiers in the UI. Excluded items are inspectable in a DisclosureGroup behind #if DEBUG only.
requirements.missing: Nothing required for this requirement.
requirements.remaining: None.
requirements.risks: None identified. test_scan_storesNothingOnItsOwn asserts the central guarantee that a scan alone writes nothing to the pantry.
requirements.caveats: Excluded items are hidden in release builds, so a user whose mushrooms were misclassified as household has no way to recover them from this screen — they would re-add by hand. That is a deliberate trade-off against a confirmation list cluttered with dishwashing tablets, and it is documented as such.

requirements.name: Add confirmed items to the pantry with per-item outcomes
requirements.description: Confirmed items go into the pantry through the existing pantry rules, and the user is told exactly what was added, what was already there, and what could not be added.
requirements.evidence: AddDetectedIngredientsUseCase is deliberately thin: it runs AddPantryItemUseCase once per confirmed draft and collects per-item outcomes, so a receipt of a dozen ingredients cannot be stopped dead by one duplicate. A draft with no usable quantity is reported as a failure rather than defaulted to a number the user never chose. AddDetectedIngredientsSummary reports addedNames, duplicateNames and failures with reasons, and renders one localised sentence via ListFormatter. ReceiptScannerViewModel removes accepted drafts so a second tap cannot re-add them, leaves rejected ones in place to be fixed, and closes the review sheet only on complete success; PantryView then reloads and shows the summary in an alert. This is the only path from a scan into the pantry — the scanner UI has no repository access of its own.
requirements.missing: Nothing required for this requirement.
requirements.remaining: None.
requirements.risks: The accepted-draft removal matches drafts to summary.addedNames by name string. If two drafts resolved to the same display name, both would be removed when only one was added. The canonical-name dedupe upstream makes this hard to reach, but the id is available and matching on it would be exact.
requirements.caveats: Reusing AddPantryItemUseCase rather than writing a second insertion path is why scan-time and hand-entry validation can never diverge.

requirements.name: End-to-end validation: photograph a receipt through to Firestore
requirements.description: A real receipt, photographed on a real device, is read, interpreted, confirmed and persisted to the signed-in user's Firestore pantry.
requirements.evidence: Every stage of this path exists in production code and the handoffs are consistent on inspection: ReceiptScannerView -> ReceiptScannerViewModel -> ScanReceiptUseCase (OCR -> parse -> interpret -> normalise -> pantry reconciliation) -> ReceiptItemReviewView -> AddDetectedIngredientsUseCase -> AddPantryItemUseCase -> FirestorePantryRepository. ScanReceiptUseCase is covered end to end by 12 tests, but with mock OCR, a mock interpreter and an in-memory pantry at both ends.
requirements.missing: Runtime evidence. Three independent prerequisites are unmet in this audit environment simultaneously: a physical device with Apple Intelligence enabled (the Simulator has no system language model), a real camera, and a live Firebase project with the rules deployed. No part of this path has been observed executing against real services.
requirements.remaining: Perform and record one documented end-to-end pass on a capable device: photograph a real grocery receipt, confirm the detected items, and verify in the Firebase console that the expected documents appear under users/{uid}/pantry with correct fields and server timestamps.
requirements.risks: This is the project's headline feature and the most consequential unverified claim in the report. Unit tests prove every stage is individually correct against doubles; they cannot prove the real OCR output is good enough to parse, that the real model echoes lines faithfully enough to match, or that the Firestore write lands.
requirements.caveats: Marked blocked rather than needs_verification because the blocker is specific, external and nameable — device hardware plus live credentials — not merely absent effort.
blockedBy: Apple Intelligence-capable physical device running iOS 26.x with the feature enabled
Live Firebase project credentials (GoogleService-Info.plist is gitignored)

requirements.name: Camera permission handling and usage description
requirements.description: Camera access is requested correctly and the purpose string accurately describes why the app needs the camera.
requirements.evidence: CameraAccess.request() checks UIImagePickerController.isSourceTypeAvailable first (returning .unavailable on a device with no camera, including the Simulator), then AVCaptureDevice.authorizationStatus, requesting on .notDetermined and treating .restricted as denied. Each outcome has an explanation and the scanner presents the camera only after .granted. NSCameraUsageDescription is present in Info.plist, so the app will not crash on first camera access.
requirements.missing: The purpose string is stale and describes the removed feature: NSCameraUsageDescription reads 'FridgeFit uses the camera to photograph the inside of your fridge so Apple Intelligence can identify ingredients on this device.' The fridge-photo scanner was replaced by receipt scanning in commit b79ee34, and the camera is now used only to photograph receipts. CameraAccess.denied carries the same stale wording ('needs camera access to photograph your fridge'), as does CameraPicker's own doc comment. No tests cover the permission logic.
requirements.remaining: Update NSCameraUsageDescription and CameraAccess.denied's explanation to describe receipt photography. Both are user-visible strings, one of them at App Store review time.
requirements.risks: A purpose string that does not match actual camera use is a recognised App Store review rejection reason, and it misleads the user at the exact moment they are deciding whether to grant access.
requirements.caveats: This is the clearest residue of the fridge-scan-to-receipt-scan migration. The permission logic itself is correct; only the wording is wrong. Fixing it means editing production files, which this audit does not do.

requirements.name: Find a substitute for an unavailable recipe ingredient
requirements.description: On a recipe's detail screen, any ingredient that is missing, insufficient or unverifiable offers a Find Substitute action that returns usable alternatives.
requirements.evidence: RecipeDetailView renders a SubstitutionSectionView beneath every ingredient whose availability is .missing, .insufficient or .quantityUnverified. The section has its own loading, results and error states and a Find Substitute button. SubstitutionViewModel keys loading, results and errors by RecipeIngredient.id so several ingredients on one recipe can be resolved independently, and surfaces a specific message when the provider returned nothing usable. SubstitutionSuggestionCard shows the app's own validation verdict, the on-hand amount, the explanation and any limitations.
requirements.missing: The feature cannot return a suggestion in this checkout. ContentView builds the substitution service from OpenRouterConfiguration.loadFromInfoPlist(), which reads OPENROUTER_API_KEY from Info.plist; that value comes from $(OPENROUTER_API_KEY), which Config.xcconfig supplies only by optionally including Secrets.xcconfig. Secrets.xcconfig is gitignored and is NOT present in the working tree, so the key resolves empty, loadFromInfoPlist returns nil, and ContentView falls back to UnconfiguredSubstitutionService. Every Find Substitute tap therefore fails with SubstitutionServiceError.notConfigured.
requirements.remaining: Create Secrets.xcconfig from Secrets.example.xcconfig with a valid OpenRouter key, rebuild, and confirm the feature returns suggestions against the live provider.
requirements.risks: A demonstration from a fresh clone of this repository will show this feature failing, not working. The failure is handled gracefully and the message names the fix, but the feature is non-functional until a key is supplied. This is a configuration gap, not a code defect.
requirements.caveats: Falling back to an explicit UnconfiguredSubstitutionService rather than sending an empty Bearer token is the correct design, and the gitignored-secret arrangement is good practice (see CD-INFRA-03).

requirements.name: OpenRouter substitution provider
requirements.description: Substitution candidates come from a remote LLM via OpenRouter's OpenAI-compatible chat completions API, with every failure mode mapped to a message written for the user.
requirements.evidence: OpenRouterSubstitutionService POSTs to https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/chat/completions with a 20-second timeout, a Bearer token and optional attribution headers. SubstitutionPromptBuilder is the single place prompt text is constructed; its system prompt restricts the model to culinary substitutions, requires 1–3 ranked suggestions, demands explicit limitations, pins an exact JSON schema and — the important rule — forbids the model from claiming the user has an ingredient or stating a pantry quantity. The response path maps 429 to .rateLimited, non-2xx to .providerUnavailable, URLError.timedOut to .timeout, other URLErrors to .network, and undecodable bodies to .malformedResponse. SubstitutionResponseParser defensively strips a markdown code fence and takes the substring between the first { and last }, tolerating stray prose, but never attempts to repair malformed JSON.
requirements.missing: The seven service tests run against a StubURLProtocol — excellent coverage of the request shape and every error branch, with no network and no quota consumed, but by construction they say nothing about the live provider. The default model (a free-tier Gemma variant) was never called, so real-world latency, refusal rate and JSON-schema compliance are unmeasured.
requirements.remaining: With a key configured (CD-SUBST-01), make a handful of real requests and record latency, how often the model honours the JSON-only instruction, and how often it tries to assert pantry availability despite the prompt.
requirements.risks: Free-tier OpenRouter models are rate-limited and can be deprecated or withdrawn; the default model string is a hardcoded fallback that will eventually go stale. This is also the only feature that sends data off-device — recipe title, target ingredient and the full pantry ingredient list, which is personal data, though SubstitutionRequest deliberately carries no ids and nothing about the Firebase user.
requirements.caveats: Testing a real HTTP client against a stubbed URLProtocol is the right technique and is applied well here. The gap is live validation, not test quality.

requirements.name: Deterministic validation of substitution suggestions against the pantry
requirements.description: Whether a suggested substitute is actually in the pantry, in sufficient quantity, and in a comparable unit is decided by the app from its own data — never by the LLM.
requirements.evidence: SubstitutionSuggestionValidator is the single place allowed to decide pantry existence, sufficiency and unit compatibility. It drops structurally invalid candidates entirely (blank name or explanation) as distinct from marking them rejected, clamps any provider confidence into 0–1, parses suggestedUnit from a raw string and treats an unparseable one as no unit given, matches the pantry with the same Ingredient.matches(name:) rule used everywhere, and assigns one of five statuses: availableInPantry, notInPantry, insufficientQuantity, unsupportedUnit (when MeasurementUnit.convert cannot safely compare), or rejected. RawSubstitutionSuggestion and SubstitutionSuggestion are separate types so the untrusted and validated shapes cannot be mixed up, and the raw type deliberately has no pantry fields at all.
requirements.missing: Nothing required for this requirement.
requirements.remaining: None.
requirements.risks: None identified. test_validate_unknownIngredient_isNeverClaimedAsAvailable and test_validate_pantryQuantityInsufficient_neverClaimsEnough assert the two adversarial cases by name.
requirements.caveats: The provider's own confidence value is carried through but is explicitly never used to decide availability — it is informational only, and the UI does not display it.

requirements.name: Deduplicate, rank, cap and cache substitution results
requirements.description: The user sees a short, ranked, duplicate-free list, pantry-backed options first, and re-opening the same prompt against an unchanged pantry does not make another provider call.
requirements.evidence: GetIngredientSubstitutionsUseCase validates every raw candidate, drops rejected and structurally invalid ones, deduplicates by lowercased trimmed name with first occurrence winning, sorts by an explicit status priority (availableInPantry, then insufficientQuantity, unsupportedUnit, notInPantry, rejected) and caps the result to three. Results are cached under a SubstitutionCacheKey of recipe id, normalised ingredient name and a hash of the pantry snapshot, so a pantry change invalidates the entry naturally with no expiry logic. The cache is checked before the provider call.
requirements.missing: Nothing required for this requirement.
requirements.remaining: None.
requirements.risks: The cache is unbounded and never evicts. Documented as acceptable for one-recipe-detail-at-a-time usage, and the process-lifetime scope limits growth, but it is a slow leak in a long session. The pantry snapshot hash relies on Hasher, whose seed is randomised per process — correct here precisely because the cache does not persist across launches, and the code says so.
requirements.caveats: The cache instance is created once in ContentView and is not cleared on sign-out, so cached suggestions could in principle outlive a user switch within one app session. The pantry-snapshot component of the key makes a stale hit unlikely rather than impossible. Related to CD-AUTH-04.

requirements.name: Dietary restriction enforcement on substitutions
requirements.description: A suggested substitute that conflicts with the user's stated dietary restrictions is never presented as usable.
requirements.evidence: The mechanism exists and is tested end to end. SubstitutionRequest carries dietaryRestrictions; SubstitutionPromptBuilder adds a 'Dietary restrictions to respect' line when the list is non-empty, and the system prompt instructs the model never to suggest a conflicting ingredient; SubstitutionSuggestionValidator.conflictsWithRestriction performs a deterministic case-insensitive substring check and marks a conflicting candidate .rejected, which GetIngredientSubstitutionsUseCase.validateAndRank then filters out so it can never reach the UI.
requirements.missing: The list is never populated in production. GetIngredientSubstitutionsUseCase.execute declares dietaryRestrictions: [String] = [], and its only production caller — SubstitutionViewModel.findSubstitutes — omits the argument entirely, so the default empty array is always used. A grep for dietaryRestrictions across the whole codebase finds it supplied non-empty only in test code. There is no dietary profile UI, no storage, and nothing to read a restriction from. The code documents this honestly as 'always empty until a future phase adds a real dietary/allergy profile'.
requirements.remaining: Build the dietary preferences profile (CD-PROFILE-03): a model, Firestore persistence, a Profile screen, and a read path from the view model into the use case. The substitution side then works with no further change.
requirements.risks: The gap is user-facing and safety-adjacent. A user with a nut allergy has no way to tell FridgeFit, and the substitution feature will suggest peanut butter. The validator's substring check is also explicitly not an allergen database — it would match 'peanut' in 'Peanut Butter' but not 'groundnut', and it is documented as deliberately simple. Any user-facing allergy claim would need a far stronger mechanism than this.
requirements.caveats: Building the enforcement mechanism before the data source is defensible sequencing, and the limitation is documented in the source rather than hidden. But as shipped, this requirement protects nobody.

requirements.name: Apply a substitution to the recipe
requirements.description: The user can accept a substitution so the recipe's feasibility is recomputed with the substitute in place of the original ingredient.
requirements.evidence: No implementation found. SubstitutionSuggestionCard is display-only — name, status, detail, explanation, limitations — with no accept action. Nothing in RecipeViewModel or EvaluateRecipeFeasibilityUseCase accepts a substitution, and the feasibility use case documents itself as doing 'no substitutions, just a deterministic comparison'.
requirements.missing: An accept action, a per-recipe substitution state, and a feasibility evaluation that can take substitutions into account.
requirements.remaining: Add an accepted-substitutions map keyed by recipe and ingredient, and extend EvaluateRecipeFeasibilityUseCase to consult it. Care is needed to keep the deterministic verdict explainable once an LLM suggestion can influence it.
requirements.risks: Today a substitution is advice the user acts on in their head. Letting a model-sourced suggestion change a 'Not makeable' verdict to 'Makeable' would put LLM output into the one judgement the app currently derives entirely from its own data — a deliberate architectural line that should be crossed consciously, if at all.
requirements.caveats: Not confirmed as a requirement. Arguably correct to leave as-is.

requirements.name: Show the signed-in account
requirements.description: The Profile tab tells the user which account they are signed in as.
requirements.evidence: ProfileView renders a person icon and 'Signed in as {email}' from authViewModel.user?.email, inside the Profile tab's NavigationStack with a navigation title.
requirements.missing: Nothing for this narrow requirement.
requirements.remaining: None.
requirements.risks: A Google account without an email on the Firebase user would render nothing at all rather than a fallback identity, since the Text is inside an if-let with no else branch.
requirements.caveats: Marked completed because the stated requirement is satisfied and the implementation is trivially inspectable. The Profile screen as a whole is 37 lines — an icon, one line of text and a Sign Out button — which is thin for a tab of the app. See CD-PROFILE-03 through CD-PROFILE-06.

requirements.name: Sign out from Profile
requirements.description: The Profile tab provides the sign-out action.
requirements.evidence: A destructive-role Sign Out button calling authViewModel.signOut().
requirements.missing: No tests; no executed runtime evidence. Tracked separately from CD-AUTH-05 because the UI placement and the auth behaviour are different concerns.
requirements.remaining: Covered by verifying CD-AUTH-05.
requirements.risks: See CD-AUTH-04 on view-model and cache lifetime across a sign-out within one app session.
requirements.caveats: No confirmation prompt.

requirements.name: Dietary preferences and restrictions profile
requirements.description: The user records dietary preferences, restrictions or allergies, which the rest of the app respects.
requirements.evidence: No implementation found. ProfileView has no settings of any kind. No dietary model, no Firestore collection and no UI exists; the only trace anywhere in the codebase is the unpopulated dietaryRestrictions parameter threaded through the substitution path (see CD-SUBST-05).
requirements.missing: Domain model, Firestore persistence at users/{uid} with matching security rules, a Profile editing screen, and a read path into GetIngredientSubstitutionsUseCase.
requirements.remaining: Model the preferences, persist them per user, add the Profile UI, and pass them from SubstitutionViewModel into the use case. The substitution side already honours them.
requirements.risks: This single absence is what makes CD-SUBST-05 inert, and it is the most load-bearing missing feature in the Profile area. It is also the only gap in this audit with a safety dimension: a user cannot tell the app about an allergy. Note that the existing keyword check is explicitly not an allergen database, so this should not be presented to users as allergy protection without a stronger mechanism.
requirements.caveats: The downstream hook already exists and is tested, so the remaining work is the profile itself rather than the enforcement.

requirements.name: Editable display name and avatar
requirements.description: The user can set a display name and profile photo.
requirements.evidence: No implementation found. ProfileView shows a static SF Symbol and the email address. No reference to displayName, photoURL or createProfileChangeRequest exists anywhere in the codebase.
requirements.missing: Profile editing UI and the Firebase profile-update calls.
requirements.remaining: Add an edit screen writing through Auth's profile change request, or store the fields in Firestore alongside the dietary profile.
requirements.risks: None.
requirements.caveats: Not confirmed as a requirement. Notably, a Google sign-in already supplies a display name and photo URL that the app currently discards.

requirements.name: Account management: change password, delete account
requirements.description: The user can change their password and delete their account together with its data.
requirements.evidence: No implementation found. Searches for updatePassword, reauthenticate and a user delete call return nothing. ProfileView's only action is Sign Out.
requirements.missing: Change-password flow with reauthentication, account deletion, and cascade deletion of the user's Firestore pantry subcollection.
requirements.remaining: Add both flows. Account deletion needs a decision about the pantry data — Firestore does not delete subcollections with a parent document, so this needs either a client-side sweep or a Cloud Function.
